segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides: Opening the Court of Chancery

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of one of the greatest, strangest, most furious novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the coming episodes we'll be moving through Dickens' extraordinary 1852 masterpiece chapter by chapter, passage by passage.
We'll be asking what the novel is actually doing — beneath the fog, beneath the melodrama, beneath the relentless comedy.
Today, we begin at the beginning: the Court of Chancery, the fog that opens the novel, and what both of them are hiding.
I'm joined by three exceptional readers of this novel, each bringing a completely different set of eyes to the text.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian whose work reads Bleak House as a precise anatomy of class power.
For Daniel, every institution in this novel — Chancery, the law, philanthropy — is a machine for protecting the rich and consuming the poor.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal historian who specializes in Victorian institutions — the man who can tell you what Chancery actually was, and what it actually did to real people.
James brings the historical record alongside the novel, and the combination is quietly devastating.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and lifelong Dickens reader who first encountered this novel as a teenager and has returned to it five times since.
Caroline reads for the experience — the rhythm, the comedy, the moments that make you stop and read a sentence twice.
Welcome to all three of you. Let's start where Dickens starts — in the fog.
What strikes me every time I return to that opening is how carefully Dickens positions the fog before he gives us a single human being.
We get the Thames, the meadows, the streets of London — and only then, buried in all of that murk, do we get the Lord Chancellor.
And the fog is not metaphor yet — or not only metaphor. It's a physical description of the Court of Chancery's effect on everything around it.
When we finally step inside the court itself, what we find is — and this is the thing — almost nothing happening.
Dickens gives us this wonderful, terrible inventory of who is actually present in the Lord Chancellor's court on that murky afternoon.

"There is the registrar below the judge, in wig and gown; and there are two or three maces, or petty-bags, or privy purses, or whatever they may be, in legal court suits. These are all yawning, for no crumb of amusement ever falls from Jarndyce and Jarndyce."
"Whatever they may be" — that parenthetical is doing enormous work.
Dickens is telling us that the court's own personnel are so arcane, so irrelevant to ordinary life, that even the narrator cannot be bothered to name them properly.
And then we meet the court's real inhabitants — the ones who have been swallowed by it.
There is the mad old woman with her reticule of paper matches. There is the prisoner who has been attempting to purge his contempt charge for what sounds like years.
And there is the man from Shropshire — who comes periodically to address the Chancellor, and who simply cannot be made to understand that Chancery does not know he exists.
That phrase — "having made his existence desolate for a quarter of a century" — is historically precise, not hyperbole.
The real Chancery suits of the era could and did run for decades, consuming entire lifetimes, entire family fortunes.
Dickens was not exaggerating. He was, if anything, being restrained.
What James is pointing to is exactly right, and I want to press on it a little — because there's something even more specific happening in that passage.
The people in the court who are not destroyed by it — the lawyers, the clerks — are described as yawning, or lingering for sport.
The ruined suitor from Shropshire is, in Dickens' own words, a source of potential "fun" for the lawyers' clerks watching him.
That is the class relation laid bare: one man's destroyed life is another man's entertainment.
But what I find most devastating is what Dickens shows us later — the physical legacy of Chancery written into the actual fabric of London.
Jarndyce — one of the most decent men in the novel — describes a street of property nominally belonging to the suit.

"It is a street of perishing blind houses, with their eyes stoned out, without a pane of glass, without so much as a window-frame, with the bare blank shutters tumbling from their hinges and falling asunder, the iron rails peeling away in flakes of rust, the chimneys sinking in, the stone steps to every door — and every door might be death's door — turning stagnant green."
"Eyes stoned out." Dickens chose that phrase.
Not boarded up. Not shuttered. Stoned out — as in, attacked, blinded, deliberately destroyed.
And then the line that lands like a verdict: "These are the Great Seal's impressions, my dear, all over England — the children know them."
The children know them. Not the lawyers. Not the judges. The children — who live in those streets, who grow up in that decay.
Chancery does not merely fail the poor. It stamps its failure onto the physical world and then moves on.
I want to come back to something in what Daniel just read, because that passage from Jarndyce is one I've never managed to get through quickly.
The sentence is structured as an accumulation — clause after clause piling up, each one a fresh detail of ruin.
You cannot read it fast. The syntax itself slows you down, forces you to look at every broken thing in turn.
And that, to me, is Dickens at his most technically brilliant — when the form enacts the content.
There is a passage later in the novel that works the same way, but even more hauntingly for me — the description of Richard walking in Lincoln's Inn.
By that point in the story, we already love Richard and we already dread what's happening to him.
And then the narrator does something quite extraordinary.

"On many such loungers have the speckled shadows of those trees often fallen; on the like bent head, the bitten nail, the lowering eye, the lingering step, the purposeless and dreamy air, the good consuming and consumed, the life turned sour."
"The good consuming and consumed." That is six words.
Six words that describe what Chancery does to a person who had genuine promise, genuine decency — Richard Carstone, specifically — but also every person who came before him.
The active and passive form together — consuming and consumed — he is doing it to himself, and it is being done to him simultaneously.
And then: "This lounger is not shabby yet, but that may come."
"Yet." One word carrying an entire future the reader can already see and Richard cannot.
That is what Dickens does better than almost anyone — he makes you grieve for someone who is still walking in sunshine.
Caroline's reading of that passage makes me want to press on the line that precedes it: "Chancery, which knows no wisdom but in precedent, is very rich in such precedents."
That is not a throwaway clause. That is a precise legal critique.
The Court of Chancery operated almost entirely on precedent — on past decisions — rather than on any fixed statutory code.
Which meant that the system's greatest expertise was in reproducing the outcomes it had always produced — ruin, delay, cost.
Dickens knew this. He was not summarising a legal textbook — he was describing a system he had watched operating on real families.
"Why should one be different from ten thousand?" — the narrator asks about Richard, and the answer, historically speaking, is that there was no mechanism by which he could be.
The system was not broken. It was working exactly as designed — for the benefit of those whose income depended on its perpetuation.
James has just said in one sentence what the novel takes eight hundred pages to demonstrate — and I mean that as a genuine compliment.
"Working exactly as designed." That is the horror.
Because the standard reading of Bleak House — the comfortable reading — is that Chancery is an aberration, a grotesque dysfunction that Dickens is holding up for reform.
But Dickens keeps showing us who benefits, and it is never the suitors. It is always the lawyers.
The fog at the novel's opening is not a symbol of confusion — it is a symbol of deliberate concealment.
It hides a transfer of wealth — from the Jarnydces, from all the suitors, into the hands of Vholes and Tulkinghorn and every lawyer in the book.
Dickens, I would argue, was more radical than he fully intended to be.
And that tension — between Dickens the reformer and Dickens the radical — is one we'll be returning to throughout this series.
But before we move on, Caroline — you mentioned the experience of reading these passages, the way the form enacts the content.
For listeners who may be coming to Bleak House for the first time — what do you say to reassure them that the fog lifts?
I say: the fog never entirely lifts, and that is precisely why you should keep reading.
Bleak House is not a novel that resolves into comfort. It resolves into truth.
And alongside all of that darkness, there is some of the funniest, most precise comic writing in Victorian literature.
Dickens never lets the gloom become unrelieved. He gives you Mr. Turveydrop — this magnificent, preposterous monument to self-regard — in the same novel as everything we've just been discussing.
He tells Caddy, his daughter-in-law, with infinite theatrical generosity:
"Do not even allow my simple requirements to be considered if they should at any time interfere with your own, my Caroline. Your necessities are greater than mine."
He offers her everything the house contains — while living entirely off her labour and her husband's earnings.
It is both hilarious and horrible, as the best Dickens always is.
Hilarious and horrible — that phrase might serve as the novel's own subtitle.
Coming up, we'll move deeper into what the fog conceals — the human cost of Chancery, measured not in pounds and shillings but in lives.
Jo, the crossing-sweeper, is waiting for us in the next segment — and none of us, I suspect, will get through it entirely unscathed.

segments.title: A System Built on Misery: The Machinery of Injustice

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart — brick by grimy brick — to see what's really holding it together.
I'm your host, and today we're going deep into what this novel does best: exposing the machinery of a system that grinds people down while calling itself respectable.
Three brilliant guides are with me today.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Bleak House as an anatomy of class power — every institution in this novel, for him, is a mechanism for protecting the rich and punishing the poor.
Professor James Blackstone brings the legal historian's eye — he knows what Chancery actually was, how it worked, and why it was so extraordinarily difficult to kill.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens — she's the one who'll remind us what it feels like to read these pages, sentence by sentence.
Our subject today is the system itself — the Court of Chancery and the culture of legal respectability that made it nearly impossible to reform.
James, you've spent a career studying Victorian institutions from the inside out — let's start with you.
What Dickens gives us in the opening pages of this novel is a portrait of Chancery that is, in its essentials, historically accurate — and that's what makes it so devastating.
The Court of Chancery by the 1850s was genuinely, structurally incapable of resolving the cases before it.
Cases could run for decades — generations — and the costs were borne entirely by the litigants, eaten alive by fees.
And yet Dickens captures something even darker than the dysfunction — he captures the attitude of the profession toward that dysfunction.
He gives us this extraordinary line very early on — let me read it because the rhythm is everything.
"Jarndyce and Jarndyce has passed into a joke. That is the only good that has ever come of it. It has been death to many, but it is a joke in the profession."
Death to many, but a joke in the profession.
That pivot — that brutal little pivot — is the whole indictment in a sentence.
And notice what the joke is doing, institutionally.
The laughter of the profession is not incidental — it is a mechanism of self-protection.
If Jarndyce and Jarndyce is a joke, then it cannot be a crime.
If every Chancellor has been in it, if every articled clerk has sharpened his wit on it — then it belongs to everyone, it is culture, it is tradition.
And tradition cannot be dismantled.
That is exactly the move Dickens shows Kenge making later with Vholes — the same sleight of hand, the same immunization through respectability.
What strikes me about that passage, every time I read it, is the precision of "tickled the maces, bags, and purses."
The maces don't laugh. The bags don't laugh. The purses certainly don't laugh.
The humans have been replaced by their instruments of office.
The joke delights not the men but the apparatus.
It's a small comic touch, but it tells you everything about how Dickens sees this world — the institution has swallowed the person whole.
James, there's another figure in the novel who finds Chancery not merely acceptable but positively constitutional — Sir Leicester Dedlock.
What's Dickens doing with that character in the context of reform?
Sir Leicester is one of the great satirical portraits in all of Dickens, and it's very precise satire.
He genuinely believes in Chancery — not because he understands it, but because he has never needed to understand it.
The passage Dickens gives us is almost unbearably funny in its logic.
"Sir Leicester has no objection to an interminable Chancery suit. It is a slow, expensive, British, constitutional kind of thing."
Slow, expensive, British, constitutional — as if those four words were synonyms.
As if the expense were part of the dignity.
And then Dickens delivers the punchline — to support any complaint about this system would be to encourage someone in the lower classes to rise up, quote, "like Wat Tyler."
There it is. The fear behind the deference. Always the fear.
That Wat Tyler reference is doing extraordinary work.
Wat Tyler led the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 — this is the spectre that haunts every Victorian aristocrat when they contemplate institutional reform.
The logic is: if you pull one brick from this wall — this slow, expensive, British wall — the whole edifice comes down.
And Sir Leicester doesn't think this cynically — he believes it, completely, which makes him far more dangerous than a cynic.
Sincere defenders of unjust systems are always more durable than corrupt ones.
I keep returning to the detail about Sir Leicester's one real grievance — it isn't the delay, it isn't the expense.
His concern is that his name is in the case but not in the title of the case.
Dickens calls it — and I love this — "a shadowy impression that for his name — the name of Dedlock — to be in a cause, and not in the title of that cause, is a most ridiculous accident."
He cannot feel the human cost of the case at all — but the injury to his name, that he feels acutely.
That's Dickens at his most wickedly exact.
Let's move from the aristocratic defender of the system to its professional enforcer — Mr. Vholes and the remarkable passage where Kenge argues that reform would destroy a class of men.
James, this is your passage — and it's extraordinary.
It is extraordinary, and it reads almost like a direct transcript of actual Parliamentary testimony — because it is.
Dickens was drawing on real blue books — Parliamentary committee reports — and the arguments being made in fiction were being made verbatim in committee rooms.
The argument is brilliant in its cynicism: we cannot reform this law because reforming it would damage the careers of those who profit from it.
Kenge puts it with a kind of magnificent effrontery — listen to this.
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth. Now you cannot afford — I will say, the social system cannot afford — to lose an order of men like Mr. Vholes."
The social system cannot afford it.
The suffering client's interest is irrelevant — the integrity of the professional class is the social good that must be protected.

And Dickens then gives us the mock Parliamentary inquiry — with that glorious question number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight hundred and sixty-nine — which is funny but also a perfect mimic of how these inquiries actually moved.
What Kenge is doing there is something very specific — he's converting a class interest into a social necessity.
Vholes is diligent, persevering, steady, acute — these are the words Kenge uses.
Victorian bourgeois virtues. The language of moral desert.
And by attributing those virtues to Vholes, Kenge makes the case that reforming the law is not merely inconvenient but morally wrong — it would punish virtue.

The Parliamentary committee version is even sharper — the question about whether these forms cause delay, cause expense, cause vexation — yes, yes, yes — but the attorney has never personally experienced any vexation.
The suffering is entirely invisible from where he stands.
And Dickens builds the whole thing to that final answer — "Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man" — which proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years.
Ten years. One answer. One name. That is the system working exactly as designed.
The mock Parliamentary inquiry is genuinely funny — that absurd question number running to nine digits — and then the humour cracks open into something awful.
Because the final answer isn't dramatic. It isn't a villain's speech.
It's just — "Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man."
And that's the end of the inquiry. For a decade.
The word "respectable" is doing the work of a whole army.
It's a fortress, not a compliment.
We've been talking about the institution as seen from above — from the lawyers, the aristocrats, the committee rooms.
But the novel also shows us the system as experienced from the very bottom — through Esther's narration, through the people swallowed by Jarndyce and Jarndyce without ever understanding what it is.
Daniel, there's a moment early in Esther's narrative — a single line from the Lord Chancellor — that tells us a great deal about how the machine processes people.
The line is almost bureaucratic in its plainness, which is exactly the point.
Esther has just arrived in Chancery — she barely understands where she is or why — and the Lord Chancellor simply says:
"The Jarndyce in question is Jarndyce of Bleak House."
A human being reduced to a file reference.
The Chancellor is still turning over leaves — that detail matters — he's still reading as he speaks, as if the case itself and the child before him exist on the same plane of administrative concern.
This is the novel's fundamental image of the law — paper processing paper, while people wait.
And what's so moving about reading that from Esther's perspective is that she records it without irony — she doesn't know enough yet to be ironic about it.
She's a child standing in a fog, literal and legal, and a man is reading from a document about her life.
The double narration that Dickens uses in this novel — Esther's intimate first person alongside the omniscient satirical narrator — is never more powerful than in these moments.
The satirist shows us the machine. Esther shows us what the machine costs.
It's worth underlining that Tulkinghorn's reading of the case preamble — "In Chancery. Between John Jarndyce" — functions the same way in the Dedlock drawing room.
The legal formula begins and Lady Dedlock nearly faints — she recognizes something in the handwriting.
The machinery of Chancery, operating perfectly normally, turns over a leaf — and a secret that will destroy lives is about to be exposed.
The system doesn't intend harm. It is simply indifferent — and indifference, at scale, is its own kind of violence.
Indifference at scale — that phrase is going to stay with me.

We've traced the machinery today from its most self-satisfied defenders — Sir Leicester, Kenge, the respectable Mr. Vholes — down to the individual human being filed away in the Lord Chancellor's papers.

In our next segment, we'll look at what this system actually produces — not the legal delays, not the fees, but the human wreckage — and the characters Dickens places in that wreckage to make us feel the cost.
We turn now to one of the novel's most painful sustained portraits: the slow collapse of Richard Carstone.
Richard begins the novel as charm itself — open, gifted, genuinely lovable.
And Dickens maps his disintegration with a precision that is almost clinical — and utterly heartbreaking.
Caroline, you've lived with this novel since your teens — what is it about Richard that gets under your skin?
Richard is the character I can never quite protect myself from.
Every re-read, I think — this time I'll hold something back.
And every time, there's this moment in chapter fifty-one that just undoes me.
Woodcourt arrives at Symond's Inn and Richard sees him — and look at what Dickens gives him to say.
"Woodcourt, my dear fellow — you come upon my vision like a ghost."
A ghost.
He uses the word himself, about a living friend walking through his door.
Dickens has already written Richard's epitaph, and Richard is the one delivering it.
That detail rewards attention, because Symond's Inn is not chosen arbitrarily.
It was one of the old Inns of Chancery — minor, decayed, haunted by failed legal careers.
Dickens plants Richard in a building whose architecture is itself a history of ruin.
And then Esther notes something that Woodcourt brings back to her — this weight of anxiety about Ada's property.
Now, what the real Chancery consumed — in documented cases, decade after decade — was precisely inherited property held by people without the legal sophistication to defend it.
Dickens knew this pattern intimately, and he names it here through Esther's quiet dread.
And that dread has a precise shape — the shape of Mr. Vholes.
Esther's fear is not vague — she names it exactly.
"My dear girl's little property would be absorbed by Mr. Vholes — and that Richard's justification to himself would be sincerely this."
Sincerely.
That word is doing devastating work.
Richard will not lie to himself — he will genuinely believe that Ada's money, spent on litigation, is an act of love and commitment.
That is what the system produces in him: a self-serving delusion he experiences as virtue.
And Skimpole — who is never without his uses as a mirror — gives us the other side of that same coin.
There's this extraordinary speech of his about Richard and Common Sense.
He imagines Common Sense as a tax-gatherer — wrinkled, prosaic, change for a ten-pound note in every pocket.

"Our dear Richard, sanguine, ardent, overleaping obstacles, bursting with poetry like a young bud — says, 'I see a golden prospect before me; it's very bright, it's very beautiful, it's very joyous; here I go, bounding over the landscape to come at it!'"
And Skimpole loves this portrait — he is enchanted by it.
But the joke turns rancid the moment you remember that Skimpole has been actively steering Richard toward Vholes.
He is celebrating the very quality in Richard that will destroy him — and collecting a fee for the introduction.
That passage is Dickens at his most politically sharp, I think — and it tends to get underread because it sounds like Skimpole simply being whimsical.
But the fees, the fraud, the horsehair wigs — Dickens is naming the actual machinery.
There were documented scandals in the 1840s and 50s in which solicitors in Chancery cases ran up costs that bore no rational relationship to the estate's value.
And the suitor — like Richard — had no legal recourse against his own lawyer.
Mr. George puts it most simply — he asks Jarndyce point-blank whether he is a Chancery suitor, and the question lands like a diagnosis.
George is interesting precisely because he has no illusions.
He has seen men come to his shooting gallery — for skill, or for idleness, he says, six of one and half a dozen of the other.
"Six of one, and half-a-dozen of the other."
It's a soldier's aphorism — pragmatic, world-weary — and George brings it to bear on Chancery with the same flatness.
The system doesn't care what brings you in — skill, idleness, hope, despair — it processes you the same way.
Richard enters with poetry bursting out of him, and the system has no more interest in that than in the horsehair wig on the judge's head.
What breaks my heart is Ada — and what Esther sees, and cannot say.
She calls it a shade — "the shade was still between me and my darling."
"The shade was still between me and my darling."
Not a wall — a shade.
Something that has crept between them — made of Richard's choices and Ada's loyalty and Esther's helplessness to stop any of it.
Dickens gives Esther this language of meteorology and shadow for everything she can't grieve directly — and it's heartbreaking precisely because it is so controlled.
That image of the shade is one I keep returning to — the novel's grief expressed through atmosphere rather than declaration.
Richard gambles everything on a case that cannot be won — and those around him can only watch.
Next, we'll look at the system that enables him — the machinery of Chancery itself, and the men who oil it.

segments.title: The Weight of Secrets: Lady Dedlock's Unraveling

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great labyrinthine novel apart, chapter by chapter, to see what's actually inside.
Today we're deep inside the world of Lady Dedlock — a character whose composure is a kind of armour, and whose secrets will eventually destroy her.
With me today are three readers who know this novel and this character with unusual intimacy.
Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and lifelong Dickens devotee who has returned to Bleak House five times and still finds new things to grieve.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads the novel as an anatomy of class power — every institution in it a mechanism for keeping someone down.

And Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who can tell you exactly what Victorian England would have made of Lady Dedlock's position — and exactly how ruthlessly it would have acted on that knowledge.
Let's begin where Dickens so often forces us to begin — with appearance.
What strikes me first about Lady Dedlock — every time I come back — is how much work her surface does.
She is performing composure so relentlessly that the performance becomes, in a strange way, its own kind of suffering.
There's a scene — one of the most quietly devastating in the novel — where Tulkinghorn has her cornered, and she knows it.
She has eaten no dinner, but she has twice or thrice poured water with a steady hand and drunk it.
"This woman," thinks Mr. Tulkinghorn, standing on the hearth, again a dark object closing up her view, "is a study."
He is clinical. He is fascinated. And she is — to him — an object.
That word — study — does so much. It means she is observed, categorised, contained.
And notice what enables his study. It's not just his intelligence — it's his institutional position.
Tulkinghorn is the legal arm of the aristocracy. He holds secrets the way the law holds debts — as instruments of control.
Lady Dedlock's composure is real — Dickens doesn't condescend to her — but it is also a class performance she has been trained to deliver since birth.
Look at how Dickens frames Sir Leicester — her husband — with the same forensic irony.
"He supposes all his dependents to be utterly bereft of individual characters, intentions, or opinions, and is persuaded that he was born to supersede the necessity of their having any."
That is the ideology of the English ruling class in a single sentence.
Lady Dedlock has lived inside that ideology so long that it has become her bones.
What Daniel says about institutional position is worth pressing on, because Tulkinghorn's power is not metaphorical — it is entirely literal.
A Victorian family solicitor of Tulkinghorn's standing held a remarkable degree of discretionary authority.
He knew property arrangements, marriage settlements, inheritance structures — the entire architecture of a family's power.
And there was no formal mechanism by which a client could compel his silence.
Privilege was precisely that — a privilege, not a right.
What Dickens renders as gothic menace — Tulkinghorn standing there like a dark object — is historically accurate menace.
That phrase — dark object closing up her view — is one I've never been able to get out of my head.
He isn't just standing in her physical sightline. He is closing up her future.
And then there's the scene where Esther first sees her mother coming through the wood.
Esther herself doesn't yet know who she's looking at — and that unknowing is exquisitely managed.
Dickens gives us — through Esther — this slow, almost cinematic revelation.
"By little and little it revealed itself to be a woman's — a lady's — Lady Dedlock's."
The grammar itself performs the recognition — three beats, each one narrowing, each one more specific.
And then — she is coming with a much quicker step than usual.
That quicker step is everything. It is the first crack in the performance.
And what's remarkable is how the housekeeper's eye catches the same fault lines in Lady Dedlock, long before any crisis.
Rosa is effusive — Lady Dedlock is so affable, so graceful, so beautiful — and Mrs. Rouncewell quietly doesn't quite agree.
"Mrs. Rouncewell is not quite sure as to that... Mrs. Rouncewell thinks she would be more affable."
And there it is — not cruelty, not condescension — just a precise, experienced judgment from below stairs.
The servant sees what the aristocrat cannot afford to see about herself.
Mrs. Rouncewell is one of Dickens' finest minor triumphs, precisely because she is given a moral authority that outranks her social station.
She can't say it plainly — Dickens gives her that circumlocution about syllables in dispraise — but the judgment is there, crystalline.
And historically, housekeepers of her standing were among the very few working people who had daily, unsupervised proximity to the aristocracy.
They saw the coldness. They saw the performance. And most of them, like Mrs. Rouncewell, kept their own counsel.
And when the performance finally gives way — when Lady Dedlock goes to Esther — it's not melodrama. It's something more devastating.
There's something I love about the contrast Dickens sets up around questions of legitimacy — who belongs, and by what right.
Jarndyce has this extraordinary speech to Mrs. Woodcourt — Esther's future mother-in-law — who is full of pedigree-snobbery.

"Come you, and see my child from hour to hour; set what you see against her pedigree, which is this, and this — for I scorned to mince it — and tell me what is the true legitimacy when you shall have quite made up your mind on that subject."
For I scorned to mince it. That parenthesis. That ferocity, slipped in between commas.
Dickens is asking — through Jarndyce — what legitimacy even means, when the legitimate world produced Lady Dedlock's tragedy.
That question — what is true legitimacy — sits at the heart of so much of what this novel does.
Lady Dedlock is the novel's great study in what happens when the world's verdict and the person's truth come catastrophically apart.
Coming up, we'll look more closely at the machinery Dickens builds around her — the law, the servants, the fog — and what it means that she never quite gets to speak for herself in her own story.

segments.title: Parallel Sufferings: Jo and Richard in the System's Grip

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been tracing the novel's great theme of institutional destruction — how systems grind people down, not through malice alone, but through indifference.
In this segment, we're looking at two very different victims caught in the system's grip: Jo the crossing sweeper, and Richard Carstone, the ward in Chancery.
Daniel Rosen has been thinking hard about what Dickens is doing when he places these two figures in parallel — and whether that parallelism is political in ways we might not expect.
Daniel, let's start with Richard.
What strikes me most about Richard is that Dickens refuses to make it simply a character flaw.
This is a novel acutely aware that people are shaped by their conditions — and Richard's condition started long before Chancery got its hooks into him.
Esther gives us the diagnosis quite precisely, and it's worth sitting with.
She says the educational system had addressed him in exactly the same manner as it had addressed hundreds of other boys, all varying in character and capacity.
There it is — the system's violence dressed as neutrality.
The system treats everyone identically, and in doing so it betrays everyone individually.
Richard isn't weak — he's been produced.
And that's not a metaphor — that's a fairly accurate description of how Victorian public education actually functioned.
The grammar schools and the larger private establishments ran on a single curriculum, a single pace, applied without regard for who was sitting in the room.
What Dickens catches — and this is characteristic — is that the system wasn't accidentally indifferent.
Uniformity was the point.
It produced a class of men who could pass examinations and occupy roles — law, church, army — without troubling anyone with inconvenient individuality.
What gets me is the sentence that follows all of that — the one Esther gives us about fire and water.
She says his good qualities were like fire and water — though excellent servants, they were very bad masters.
Like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were very bad masters.
That's such a compressed and beautiful formulation.
It's classical in structure — it almost sounds like a proverb — and yet Dickens has loaded it with genuine sadness.
Because Richard's gifts are real.
The tragedy isn't that he's talentless — it's that his talents have been turned against him.
And Chancery completes what the school system started.
By the time we reach the later stages of Richard's deterioration, he has achieved something that the novel presents almost as a logical endpoint.
He no longer sees a lawsuit — he sees a person.
He tells Vholes — and this is devastating — that Jarndyce becomes to him the embodiment of the suit.
He becomes to me the embodiment of the suit; that in place of its being an abstraction, it is John Jarndyce.
He has transferred his entire psychic world onto a human target.
The system has taught him to look for enemies, and now he finds them in the one man who genuinely loves him.
Gridley gets there first, though — and more ferociously.
Gridley is what Richard will become if Richard lives long enough — and what the novel won't permit Richard to become, because the sentimental logic demands a quieter death.
But Gridley's rage is instructive.
He has been to prison for contempt of court, for threatening solicitors — all because he will not be pacified.
And he explains why, with terrible clarity, when he says — I must have this vent under my sense of injury, or nothing could hold my wits together.
I must have this vent under my sense of injury or nothing could hold my wits together.
His anger isn't pathology — it's self-preservation.
Take the anger away, and there is nothing left.
And then there's the image he gives of his own death — which is one of the most extraordinary things in the whole novel.
He says that if he knew when he was going to die, and could be carried into court, he would die there saying something.
You have brought me here and sent me from here many and many a time. Now send me out feet foremost.
Feet foremost.
That's how you carry a corpse.
He's saying: the only way you're getting rid of me is as a dead man.
It's defiance and grief at once, and Dickens lands it in four words.
And what Chancery says back to all of this — Gridley's rage, Richard's ruin — is essentially nothing.
Mr. Kenge's response to the entire catastrophe of Jarndyce and Jarndyce is one of the novel's blackest jokes.
He describes it with magnificent self-satisfaction as a monument of Chancery practice.
A monument of Chancery practice.
A monument — to what exactly?
To the careers it sustained.
To the fees extracted from an estate until there was nothing left.
Richard and Gridley are not unfortunate exceptions — they are the system working exactly as designed.
Kenge's phrase is genuinely chilling once you know what lies behind it.
The real Court of Chancery in the 1840s and 1850s had cases that had run for decades — some since the previous century.
Estates were consumed entirely by legal costs before a judgment was ever reached.
Dickens knew this — and so did his readers.
What he adds is the figure of Kenge, who speaks of it as an achievement — smoothly, persuasively, with his silver trowel.
The silver trowel is Dickens at his most precise — a man plastering over atrocity with elaborate, self-congratulatory prose.
So we have education producing a Richard who cannot direct his own gifts, and Chancery finishing the work.
And we have Gridley — who resists, who rages, and whose rage is the only honest response the novel permits.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the figure who receives no such response at all — Jo, the crossing sweeper, who is moved on until there is nowhere left to go.

segments.title: Wit and Darkness: Comic Relief in a Blighted World

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens apart sentence by sentence and put him back together — slightly winded.
Today's segment is about something Dickens does that nobody else quite manages: the comedy that makes the darkness darker.
With me are Daniel Rosen, cultural historian and our resident anatomist of class power — who sees the joke as a delivery mechanism for the knife.
James Blackstone, legal historian, who knows exactly what these Victorian institutions actually were — and finds Dickens unsettlingly accurate.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and devoted re-reader, who will remind us what it feels like to encounter these passages for the first time — and the fifth.
Let's start with Krook — the rag-and-bottle man who calls himself the Lord Chancellor's brother.
Daniel, Krook is clearly a comic figure — and yet there's something genuinely sinister in his comedy.
Krook is one of Dickens' great structural jokes — and I mean structural in a precise sense.
He is the Court of Chancery in miniature — the hoarding, the refusal to clean, the absolute grip on everything he's ever touched.
And Dickens lets Krook say it himself, which is the audacious move.
Listen to how he puts it — he says:

"I don't mind. I go to see my noble and learned brother pretty well every day, when he sits in the Inn. He don't notice me, but I notice him. There's no great odds betwixt us. We both grub on in a muddle."
He don't notice me, but I notice him — that's the whole satirical structure of the novel in eleven words.
The powerful don't see the poor. The poor see everything. And the joke is that they're the same.
What gets me every time is the rhythm of that speech — the way it accumulates.
"I have so many things here... of so many kinds... wasting away and going to rack and ruin."
It piles up like Krook's shop itself — clause after clause, hoarded, uncleared.
And then the sudden intimacy: "Hi, Lady Jane!"
That exclamation punctures everything — the gothic menace, the satirical weight — and you're just left with a peculiar old man and his cat.
That's what makes Dickens so hard to describe to someone who hasn't read him. The tonal range is impossible.
The comedy is real, but the target is very precise — and historically, Dickens is being almost documentary here.
The real Court of Chancery by the 1850s was essentially Krook's shop with marble columns.
Cases accumulating for decades. Documents misfiled. Estates consumed entirely by costs before a judgment was ever issued.
The joke "We both grub on in a muddle" is funny until you realise the muddle is people's lives.
And then Dickens does something even more unsettling — he introduces the gothic register without abandoning the comic one.
In the very next chapter, Esther is confronted with those words — written and erased on the floor:
"When I told him, he laughed. In the same odd way, yet with the same rapidity, he then produced singly, and rubbed out singly, the letters forming the words Bleak House."
"These, in some astonishment, I also read; and he laughed again."
That laugh is doing extraordinary work. It's comedic — Krook is eccentric, almost farcical — but it's also a threat.
He knows who Esther is before she does. The laugh is the novel's secret, laughing at her.
"He laughed again" — three words, and the hairs on your neck stand up.
On a first reading you think it's comic texture — the old man is strange and funny.
On the second reading you realise it's the most sinister sentence in the chapter.
That's the Dickens double exposure — the image develops in retrospect, and it changes colour entirely.
Can we turn to Skimpole? Because I think he's the novel's most troubling comic creation — more troubling than Krook, actually.
Krook's comedy is satirical — it targets an institution. Skimpole's comedy targets a moral evasion that is very much still with us.
Here he is, explaining why Chancery's abuses are actually rather charming — he says:
"Some ill-conditioned growling fellow may say to me, 'What's the use of these legal and equitable abuses? How do you defend them?'"
"I reply, 'My growling friend, I DON'T defend them, but they are very agreeable to me.'"
The nerve of it is breathtaking. He doesn't deny the abuse — he simply relocates himself outside accountability.
And the comedy is the camouflage. You laugh at the absurdity of the position — and while you're laughing, you've been told something true.
Skimpole is where Dickens gets genuinely radical, I think — more so than he perhaps intended.
Because Skimpole isn't stupid. He has a complete ideology — the aesthete who exempts himself from the claims of the suffering.
He says he is "a child among you worldly grumblers" — not called upon to account for anything.
That is the position of every privileged person who has ever called politics "dreary" or charity "tiresome."
The comedy makes him delightful in the room — and completely monstrous in the world.
The thing that strikes me about Skimpole is the pastoral imagery he deploys — Richard as a shepherd, Fortune dancing through the Inns of Court.
It's gorgeous language in service of something utterly hollow.
"This present shepherd, our pastoral Richard, brightens the dull Inns of Court by making Fortune and her train sport through them."
The beauty of the prose is the con. Skimpole seduces you with the sentence — and Dickens knows you'll be seduced.
He's implicating the reader in Skimpole's charm, which is quite a wicked thing to do.
And Richard is the one who pays. Richard, who has been told this is all poetry and pastoral — ends up destroyed by Chancery.
Skimpole's comedy has a body count. That's the dark arithmetic Dickens is running throughout the novel.
That phrase — "the comedy has a body count" — feels like the thesis of the whole segment.
Before we close, there's one more moment I want to look at — a comedy of a quieter, more domestic kind.
Caroline, there's a small exchange in chapter sixty — Jarndyce and Esther and the question of Mrs. Woodcourt — that I think you've always had a soft spot for.
I do. It's tiny, and it's perfect.
By this point in the novel everything has been resolved — Esther and Woodcourt are understood to be in love, Jarndyce has accepted it with extraordinary grace.
And then Jarndyce turns to Esther and says — and do notice the timing of this:
"Very good. He has made his protest, and Dame Durden has made hers, and there is nothing more to be said about it. Now I come to Mrs. Woodcourt. How do you like her, my dear?"
He pivots straight from the great emotional resolution to — well, what do you make of your future mother-in-law?
It's so human. The bathos is the love — the way he refuses to dwell in the sentimental moment.
And "Dame Durden" — that nickname, used at this moment — is almost unbearably tender.
It's worth saying that Jarndyce's generosity here is structural too, not just personal.
He is one of the very few characters in the novel who actually uses his institutional power — his guardian role, his money — to give rather than to take.
In a novel full of systems designed to extract, Jarndyce is an anomaly. And the comedy in that exchange is the comedy of decency — which is its own kind of surprise.
The comedy of decency — I love that phrase. It might be the rarest register in the novel.
From Krook's knowing laugh to Skimpole's dazzling evasions to Jarndyce's quiet pivot — Dickens uses comedy to tell us what kind of world this is and what it costs to live in it with any integrity.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at the novel's treatment of childhood and what it means to grow up — or fail to — in Bleak House's shadow.

segments.title: Synthesis: The Fog Remains—What Dickens Demands of Us

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the fog, the mud, the drip of rain on stone.
But as we reach the close, I want to ask all three of you a harder question.
What does Dickens actually demand of us — as readers, as citizens, as people living inside institutions not entirely unlike his?
Caroline, I'd like to start with you — and with Lady Dedlock at her window.
There's a passage early in the novel that I keep returning to — and I think it holds the whole book in miniature.
Dickens gives us Lady Dedlock at her window in Lincolnshire, looking out at the rain.
"The view from my Lady Dedlock's own windows is alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink."
That sentence is almost unbearably precise.
Two shades of grey — both of them colourless, both of them suffocating.
And then Dickens turns the knife.
Lady Dedlock looks out and sees a child running through the rain to meet a man coming home.
Warmth, domesticity, love — the ordinary life she has foreclosed in herself — and it puts her out of temper.
What Dickens demands, I think, is that we look at what we've trained ourselves not to feel.
That's exactly right — and I'd push it further.
Because Dickens shows us that Lady Dedlock's insensibility isn't personal weakness — it's class formation.
There's a passage I find deeply uncomfortable in the best possible way — about how the fashionable world actually works.
"Who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput."
The jewellers, the mercers, the librarians — they manage the aristocracy like livestock.
Lady Dedlock believes she is inscrutable, beyond the reach of ordinary mortals.
Every person in her orbit has mapped her vanities with clinical precision.
What Dickens is anatomising is how power sustains itself by making its beneficiaries believe they are free.
The demand he makes of us is to see the machinery — not just the gilt on top of it.
And the gilt is so beautifully rendered that you have to resist its pull even as you admire it.
That's Dickens' peculiar genius — he makes the corrupt world gorgeous, and then indicts it.
If I may — I think the sharpest formulation of what Dickens demands comes not from the grand satirical set-pieces, but from Krook's shop.
There's a moment where Krook recounts the fate of Tom Jarndyce — a man consumed by the Chancery suit — and the language is almost clinical in its horror.
"It's being ground to bits in a slow mill; it's being roasted at a slow fire; it's being stung to death by single bees; it's being drowned by drops; it's going mad by grains."
Five separate images of incremental destruction.
Not a catastrophe — a process.
And that is precisely how the Victorian legal system worked — not through spectacular cruelty, but through attrition.
Fees accumulating, years passing, will to live gradually surrendered.
Tom Jarndyce ends up shooting himself in a coffee house near Chancery Lane.
Dickens' demand, as I read it, is that we refuse the comfort of calling this historical.
The grinding by grains — that's the novel's central political image.
It's not the villain with a face.
It's the system that has no face — that processes human beings as though they were raw material.
Dickens understood this more deeply than most political economists of his time, and he expressed it in sensation rather than argument.
And sensation is what makes it survive — not the polemic, but the drip, drip, drip on the flagstones.
I keep thinking about Miss Flite's gratitude toward Woodcourt — that small, warm moment in a novel full of cold vastness.
Esther says, simply: "She is a most affectionate creature, as I have reason to say."
It's almost nothing — one sentence, barely a footnote to the plot.
And yet Dickens plants these small human recognitions throughout — insisting that tenderness is real even when the institutions are monstrous.
That's his demand, I think — not despair, but witness.
Witness — that feels exactly right as a closing word for Bleak House.
A novel that refuses to let us look away — from the fog, from the court, from the child running through the rain.
My thanks to Daniel Rosen, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has been, in the best Dickensian spirit, both capacious and precise.
Bleak House Unpacked will return.
Until then — keep reading slowly, and keep your eyes on the fog.

c1:p6.text:
Who happen to be in the Lord Chancellor’s court this murky afternoon
besides the Lord Chancellor, the counsel in the cause, two or three
counsel who are never in any cause, and the well of solicitors before
mentioned? There is the registrar below the judge, in wig and gown;
and there are two or three maces, or petty-bags, or privy purses, or
whatever they may be, in legal court suits. These are all yawning,
for no crumb of amusement ever falls from Jarndyce and Jarndyce (the
cause in hand), which was squeezed dry years upon years ago. The
short-hand writers, the reporters of the court, and the reporters of
the newspapers invariably decamp with the rest of the regulars when
Jarndyce and Jarndyce comes on. Their places are a blank. Standing on
a seat at the side of the hall, the better to peer into the curtained
sanctuary, is a little mad old woman in a squeezed bonnet who is
always in court, from its sitting to its rising, and always expecting
some incomprehensible judgment to be given in her favour. Some say
she really is, or was, a party to a suit, but no one knows for
certain because no one cares. She carries some small litter in a
reticule which she calls her documents, principally consisting of
paper matches and dry lavender. A sallow prisoner has come up, in
custody, for the half-dozenth time to make a personal application “to
purge himself of his contempt,” which, being a solitary surviving
executor who has fallen into a state of conglomeration about accounts
of which it is not pretended that he had ever any knowledge, he is
not at all likely ever to do. In the meantime his prospects in life
are ended. Another ruined suitor, who periodically appears from
Shropshire and breaks out into efforts to address the Chancellor at
the close of the day’s business and who can by no means be made to
understand that the Chancellor is legally ignorant of his existence
after making it desolate for a quarter of a century, plants himself
in a good place and keeps an eye on the judge, ready to call out “My
Lord!” in a voice of sonorous complaint on the instant of his rising.
A few lawyers’ clerks and others who know this suitor by sight linger
on the chance of his furnishing some fun and enlivening the dismal
weather a little.
c1:p6.summary: The court contains a miscellany of tragic figures: a mad woman with paper-match 'documents,' a prisoner repeatedly attempting to clear contempt charges, and a ruined suitor from Shropshire who periodically appears to plead to an indifferent Chancellor.

c8:p24.text:
“Bleak House; true. There is, in that city of London there, some
property of ours which is much at this day what Bleak House was then;
I say property of ours, meaning of the suit’s, but I ought to call it
the property of costs, for costs is the only power on earth that will
ever get anything out of it now or will ever know it for anything but
an eyesore and a heartsore. It is a street of perishing blind houses,
with their eyes stoned out, without a pane of glass, without so much
as a window-frame, with the bare blank shutters tumbling from their
hinges and falling asunder, the iron rails peeling away in flakes of
rust, the chimneys sinking in, the stone steps to every door (and
every door might be death’s door) turning stagnant green, the very
crutches on which the ruins are propped decaying. Although Bleak
House was not in Chancery, its master was, and it was stamped with
the same seal. These are the Great Seal’s impressions, my dear, all
over England—the children know them!”
c8:p24.summary: Jarndyce describes a street of property nominally belonging to the Jarndyce suit but effectively owned by costs; the houses are in terrible decay, windowless, rusted, and desolate, bearing the Great Seal's mark of Chancery throughout England.
c8:p24.best_quote: It is a street of perishing blind houses, with their eyes stoned out, without a pane of glass, without so much as a window-frame, with the bare blank shutters tumbling from their hinges and falling asunder, the iron rails peeling away in flakes of rust, the chimneys sinking in, the stone steps to every door (and every door might be death's door) turning stagnant green

c39:p43.text:
Richard, emerging from the heavy shade of Symond’s Inn into the
sunshine of Chancery Lane—for there happens to be sunshine there
to-day—walks thoughtfully on, and turns into Lincoln’s Inn, and
passes under the shadow of the Lincoln’s Inn trees. On many such
loungers have the speckled shadows of those trees often fallen; on
the like bent head, the bitten nail, the lowering eye, the lingering
step, the purposeless and dreamy air, the good consuming and
consumed, the life turned sour. This lounger is not shabby yet, but
that may come. Chancery, which knows no wisdom but in precedent, is
very rich in such precedents; and why should one be different from
ten thousand?
c39:p43.summary: Richard emerges into sunshine and walks through Lincoln's Inn, but the narrator reflects on how the space has witnessed the deterioration of many Chancery suitors before him, suggesting he may follow the same path.

c50:p32.text:
“Charming! We must take care of our dear Caroline, Miss Summerson. We
must spare nothing that will restore her. We must nourish her. My
dear Caroline”—he would turn to his daughter-in-law with infinite
generosity and protection—“want for nothing, my love. Frame a wish
and gratify it, my daughter. Everything this house contains,
everything my room contains, is at your service, my dear. Do not,” he
would sometimes add in a burst of deportment, “even allow my simple
requirements to be considered if they should at any time interfere
with your own, my Caroline. Your necessities are greater than mine.”
c50:p32.summary: Mr. Turveydrop addresses Caddy with exaggerated generosity, offering everything the house contains while framing his own needs as secondary, all delivered with theatrical grace.

c1:p8.text:
Jarndyce and Jarndyce has passed into a joke. That is the only good
that has ever come of it. It has been death to many, but it is a joke
in the profession. Every master in Chancery has had a reference out
of it. Every Chancellor was “in it,” for somebody or other, when he
was counsel at the bar. Good things have been said about it by
blue-nosed, bulbous-shoed old benchers in select port-wine committee
after dinner in hall. Articled clerks have been in the habit of
fleshing their legal wit upon it. The last Lord Chancellor handled it
neatly, when, correcting Mr. Blowers, the eminent silk gown who said
that such a thing might happen when the sky rained potatoes, he
observed, “or when we get through Jarndyce and Jarndyce, Mr.
Blowers”—a pleasantry that particularly tickled the maces, bags, and
purses.
c1:p8.summary: The legal profession treats Jarndyce and Jarndyce as an endless source of witty commentary and profit; even the Lord Chancellor has made pleasantries about it, including a quip that 'tickled the maces, bags, and purses.'
c1:p8.best_quote: Jarndyce and Jarndyce has passed into a joke. That is the only good that has ever come of it. It has been death to many, but it is a joke in the profession.

c39:p4.text:
But not perceiving this quite plainly—only seeing it by halves in a
confused way—the laity sometimes suffer in peace and pocket, with a
bad grace, and DO grumble very much. Then this respectability of Mr.
Vholes is brought into powerful play against them. “Repeal this
statute, my good sir?” says Mr. Kenge to a smarting client. “Repeal
it, my dear sir? Never, with my consent. Alter this law, sir, and
what will be the effect of your rash proceeding on a class of
practitioners very worthily represented, allow me to say to you, by
the opposite attorney in the case, Mr. Vholes? Sir, that class of
practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth. Now you
cannot afford—I will say, the social system cannot afford—to lose
an order of men like Mr. Vholes. Diligent, persevering, steady, acute
in business. My dear sir, I understand your present feelings against
the existing state of things, which I grant to be a little hard in
your case; but I can never raise my voice for the demolition of a
class of men like Mr. Vholes.” The respectability of Mr. Vholes has
even been cited with crushing effect before Parliamentary committees,
as in the following blue minutes of a distinguished attorney’s
evidence. “Question (number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight
hundred and sixty-nine): If I understand you, these forms of practice
indisputably occasion delay? Answer: Yes, some delay. Question: And
great expense? Answer: Most assuredly they cannot be gone through for
nothing. Question: And unspeakable vexation? Answer: I am not
prepared to say that. They have never given ME any vexation; quite
the contrary. Question: But you think that their abolition would
damage a class of practitioners? Answer: I have no doubt of it.
Question: Can you instance any type of that class? Answer: Yes. I
would unhesitatingly mention Mr. Vholes. He would be ruined.
Question: Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a respectable
man? Answer:”—which proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years—“Mr.
Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man.”
c39:p4.summary: Mr. Kenge's rhetorical defense of legal practitioners like Vholes is presented, along with a mock parliamentary inquiry that demonstrates how institutional self-interest defeats reform through the invocation of Vholes's respectable reputation.
c39:p4.best_quote: Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth.

c2:p19.text:
Sir Leicester has no objection to an interminable Chancery suit. It
is a slow, expensive, British, constitutional kind of thing. To be
sure, he has not a vital interest in the suit in question, her part
in which was the only property my Lady brought him; and he has a
shadowy impression that for his name—the name of Dedlock—to be in a
cause, and not in the title of that cause, is a most ridiculous
accident. But he regards the Court of Chancery, even if it should
involve an occasional delay of justice and a trifling amount of
confusion, as a something devised in conjunction with a variety of
other somethings by the perfection of human wisdom for the eternal
settlement (humanly speaking) of everything. And he is upon the whole
of a fixed opinion that to give the sanction of his countenance to
any complaints respecting it would be to encourage some person in the
lower classes to rise up somewhere—like Wat Tyler.
c2:p19.summary: Sir Leicester accepts the Chancery suit's interminable nature as a properly British institution, regarding even its inefficiency as part of the constitutional order; his main concern is that his name be prominent in the title.
c2:p19.best_quote: he has a shadowy impression that for his name—the name of Dedlock—to be in a cause, and not in the title of that cause, is a most ridiculous accident

c3:p127.text:
“The Jarndyce in question,” said the Lord Chancellor, still turning
over leaves, “is Jarndyce of Bleak House.”
c3:p127.summary: The Lord Chancellor identifies the Jarndyce estate in question as Jarndyce of Bleak House.

c2:p23.summary: Tulkinghorn begins reading the formal preamble of the Chancery case: 'In Chancery. Between John Jarndyce—'

c51:p21.text:
“Woodcourt, my dear fellow,” cried Richard, starting up with extended
hands, “you come upon my vision like a ghost.”
c51:p21.summary: Richard enthusiastically welcomes Woodcourt, comparing his sudden appearance to a ghostly visitation.

c51:p37.text:
Afterwards, when Mr. Woodcourt came to reflect on what had passed, he
was so very much impressed by the strength of Richard’s anxiety on
this point that in telling me generally of his first visit to
Symond’s Inn he particularly dwelt upon it. It revived a fear I had
had before that my dear girl’s little property would be absorbed by
Mr. Vholes and that Richard’s justification to himself would be
sincerely this. It was just as I began to take care of Caddy that the

c37:p115.text:
“Do you think so!” returned Mr. Skimpole. “Don’t say that, don’t say
that. Let us suppose him keeping company with Common Sense—an
excellent man—a good deal wrinkled—dreadfully practical—change for
a ten-pound note in every pocket—ruled account-book in his
hand—say, upon the whole, resembling a tax-gatherer. Our dear
Richard, sanguine, ardent, overleaping obstacles, bursting with
poetry like a young bud, says to this highly respectable companion,
‘I see a golden prospect before me; it’s very bright, it’s very
beautiful, it’s very joyous; here I go, bounding over the landscape
to come at it!’ The respectable companion instantly knocks him down
with the ruled account-book; tells him in a literal, prosaic way that
he sees no such thing; shows him it’s nothing but fees, fraud,
horsehair wigs, and black gowns. Now you know that’s a painful
change—sensible in the last degree, I have no doubt, but
disagreeable. I can’t do it. I haven’t got the ruled account-book, I
have none of the tax-gathering elements in my composition, I am not
at all respectable, and I don’t want to be. Odd perhaps, but so it
is!”
c37:p115.summary: Vholes admits Richard's attendance will not help, yet offers no objection.

c48:p105.text:
For a little while they are silent. Lady Dedlock has eaten no dinner,
but has twice or thrice poured out water with a steady hand and drunk
it. She rises from table, takes a lounging-chair, and reclines in it,
shading her face. There is nothing in her manner to express weakness

c48:p105.summary: In the silence that follows, Lady Dedlock maintains thoughtful composure while remaining emotionally turbulent; Tulkinghorn regards her as a fascinating psychological study.
